We eventually decided to share a home while I was in the city. I had somewhat more money than he did, so he allowed me to pay the rent and furnishings. We chose an unusual, crumbling mansion in a quiet, deserted part of the Faubourg St. Germain. People had abandoned it long ago because of superstitions we never bothered to investigate. We furnished it in a style that suited the fanciful gloom of our shared temperament.

Had anyone known how we lived there, they would have thought us mad, though perhaps harmless. We shut ourselves away completely and received no visitors. I carefully kept our address secret from my former acquaintances. As for Dupin, he had long since stopped knowing people in Paris or being known by them. We lived entirely in our own private world.

My friend had an odd passion—what else should I call it?—for night simply because it was night. I quietly took up this strange habit, as I did all his others, giving myself freely to his wild ideas. The dark goddess could not stay with us all the time, but we could imitate her presence. At the first light of morning, we closed all the old house’s untidy shutters and lit two strongly scented candles. They cast only the weakest, most ghostly light. By that light we filled our minds with dreams, reading, writing, and talking until the clock told us that true darkness had arrived. Then we went into the streets arm in arm. We continued our earlier conversations or wandered through the city until late, finding endless mental excitement in quietly observing its crowds and shifting lights and shadows.

On these outings, I could not help noticing and admiring Dupin’s unusual gift for analysis. His rich imagination had already led me to expect such an ability. He seemed to take great pleasure in using it, even if not exactly in displaying it, and willingly admitted how much he enjoyed it. With a quiet chuckle, he boasted that most people seemed to him to have windows into their hearts. He often followed this claim with startling demonstrations of how well he understood mine. At such times, he grew cold and withdrawn. His eyes had an empty look, and his voice rose from its usual warm tenor to a much higher pitch. It might have sounded irritable if he had not spoken so slowly, carefully, and clearly.

At the top of the stairs he regained his composure and decided to unleash his famous burst of demonic laughter. It had proved extremely useful on several occasions. Rumor credited it with turning Lord Raker’s wig gray overnight, and it had certainly persuaded three of Lady Canterville’s French governesses to resign before completing a month. So he gave his most horrifying laugh, making the old vaulted roof echo repeatedly. The last dreadful echoes had barely faded when a door opened and Mrs. Otis appeared in a pale blue dressing gown. “I’m afraid you’re quite unwell,” she said, “so I’ve brought you some of Dr. Dobell’s tincture. If it’s indigestion, you’ll find this an excellent remedy.” The ghost glared furiously and immediately prepared to transform himself into a large black dog. He was justly celebrated for this accomplishment, which the family doctor always blamed for the permanent mental incapacity of Lord Canterville’s uncle, the Honorable Thomas Horton. Approaching footsteps made him reconsider his terrible intention. Instead, he glowed faintly and vanished with a deep, graveyard groan just as the twins reached him.

Back in his room, he broke down completely, overcome by violent distress. The twins’ vulgarity and Mrs. Otis’s crude materialism were naturally infuriating, but what upset him most was his failure to wear the armor. He had hoped that even modern Americans would be moved by the sight of a Spectre in Armour, if only out of respect for their national poet Longfellow. He himself had passed many weary hours reading Longfellow’s graceful, appealing poetry while the Cantervilles were in London. Besides, the armor was his own. He had worn it with great success at the Kenilworth tournament and received lavish compliments from no less a person than the Virgin Queen. Yet when he put it on now, the enormous breastplate and steel helmet had overwhelmed him with their weight. He fell heavily onto the stone floor, badly scraping both knees and bruising the knuckles of his right hand.

For several days afterward he was very ill and hardly left his room, except to maintain the bloodstain properly. With careful attention to his health, however, he recovered and resolved to make a third attempt at frightening the United States Minister and his family.

“He was placed in your charge. You perceive that I know the circumstances?”

“That is indeed the fact,” Defarge answered. While knitting and humming, his wife had communicated by an apparently chance touch of her elbow that he should reply, but keep his answers short.

“His daughter came to you,” the spy continued, “and took him from your care, accompanied by a tidy gentleman in brown—what is his name?—wearing a small wig—Lorry, from Tellson and Company’s bank—and brought him to England.”

“That is the fact,” Defarge said again.

“What interesting recollections!” observed the spy. “I have met Doctor Manette and his daughter in England.”

“Indeed?” said Defarge.

“You seldom hear of them these days?” asked the spy.

“No,” replied Defarge.

“In truth,” madame interrupted, looking up from her knitting and quiet song, “we hear nothing of them. We were informed of their safe arrival, and received perhaps one further letter, perhaps two. Since then they have gradually followed their path through life, and we ours, without correspondence.”

“Quite so, madame,” the spy replied. “She is about to marry.”

“About to?” repeated madame. “She was pretty enough to have married long since. You English seem cold to me.”

“Oh! You know that I am English.”

“I hear that your tongue is,” said madame. “And I presume the man is what his tongue is.”

He did not regard this recognition as flattering, but made the best of it and laughed it aside. Draining the last of his cognac, he continued:

“Yes, Miss Manette will marry, though not an Englishman. Her husband, like herself, was born French. Speaking of Gaspard—poor Gaspard! How cruel it was, how cruel!—it is curious that she is to wed the nephew of Monsieur the Marquis, on whose account Gaspard was raised so many feet into the air. That is to say, the present Marquis. He lives unrecognized in England, however, and bears no title there, calling himself Mr. Charles Darnay. His mother’s family name was D’Aulnais.”

Madame Defarge’s knitting continued evenly, but her husband was visibly affected. Whatever he attempted behind the small counter, striking a light or lighting his pipe, his uneasiness betrayed him and his hand shook. No competent spy could have overlooked or forgotten it.

Having scored at least this single success, whatever its eventual value, and with no customers arriving to offer further opportunities, Mr. Barsad paid his bill and departed. Before leaving, he politely remarked that he anticipated the pleasure of another meeting with Monsieur and Madame Defarge.
